title: How to Catch MEP Scope Gaps Between Drawings and Specs Before Bid Day
summary: MEP scope gaps between drawings and specs cost GCs six figures per project. Here's how estimators catch them before bid day.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- MEP scope gaps between drawings and specs are the most expensive trade-level misses in commercial GC pre-construction.
- The root cause is almost always a coordination failure, not a drafting error. Drawings and specs are authored by different people on different timelines.
- A 2018 study by PlanGrid and FMI put U.S. rework from miscommunication and bad project data at $31.3 billion. MEP is the single biggest contributor.
- A $300K lead-lined glass miss on a hospital imaging suite and recurring six-figure generator conditioning disputes are documented examples from real GC bids.
- This article walks through where MEP gaps hide, how to find them systematically, and how to protect your bid before scope sheets go to subs.


MEP scope gaps are not a mechanical problem. They are a coordination problem. The architect draws a detail. The mechanical engineer specifies a system. The electrical engineer notes a requirement. Nobody reconciles all three against the same scope baseline before bid day.


That is how a hospital imaging suite ends up with $300K in lead-lined glass missing from the GC's scope. The specification called it out. The drawings showed the room layout. No one read both documents together and wrote the requirement into the scope package before it went to subs.


This happens on almost every complex MEP project. The question is whether your team catches it before bid day or absorbs it in the field.


## Why MEP Gaps Are Worse Than Other Trade Gaps


MEP is the trade cluster where drawing-to-spec conflicts are most common and most expensive. Here is why.


First, MEP work spans three disciplines (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) plus controls, fire protection, and sometimes a fourth in building automation. Each discipline has its own engineer, its own drawing set, and its own specification sections. Conflicts between them are almost guaranteed on anything above a simple renovation.


Second, MEP specification sections are where the "readily inferable" trap is deepest. Spec writers include system performance requirements, equipment standards, and testing protocols that do not appear anywhere on the drawings. Subs read the drawings. They often skim the specs. That gap is where six-figure change orders are born.


Third, MEP scopes are highly sensitive to addenda. A generator spec change in Addendum 3 that overrides the original equipment schedule is easy to miss when your team is cross-referencing 2,000 pages of bid documents in the final 72 hours before bid day.


## The Six Most Expensive MEP Scope Gaps


These are the specific items that appear most often in the GC interviews and project reviews that form the basis of[Provision's Scope Gap Playbook chapter on trade-specific gaps](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) . Each one is recoverable if caught before the scope sheet goes out. Each one is expensive if it surfaces during buyout or in the field.


### 1. Generator Field Conditioning


This is the most frequently cited MEP gap in operator interviews. Generator specifications often include field conditioning requirements: load bank testing, runtime hours, and startup commissioning by a factory-certified technician. These items do not appear on the electrical drawings. They are buried in Division 26 or Division 33 spec sections.


When the scope goes to the electrical sub without those requirements, the sub prices the equipment and rough-in. The field conditioning cost sits unpriced. One estimating manager at a Canadian ICI GC described recurring disputes totaling "millions" across multiple hospital and institutional projects where generator conditioning was not clearly assigned.


### 2. Motor Starters and Variable Frequency Drives


The mechanical drawings show equipment. The electrical drawings show power connections. Neither consistently shows who supplies and installs motor starters and VFDs. The spec sections for each discipline claim it differently, or the division of responsibility is left ambiguous.


This is a classic MEP interface gap. The mechanical sub says it is electrical scope. The electrical sub says it was not in their bid. The GC absorbs the cost or fights a change order through project delivery.


### 3. Fire-Rated Louvres


Mechanical drawings show louvre locations and sizes. The spec requires fire-rated assemblies with specific UL listings. The architectural drawings show the exterior aesthetic. None of the three consistently call out the supplier or installer.


Fire-rated louvres are specialty items with long lead times and specific structural backing requirements. Missing them at bid means a procurement crisis and a schedule impact in addition to the cost gap.


### 4. The Trench


Plumbing drawings show drain locations. Civil or structural drawings show slab details. Neither reliably assigns responsibility for the trench: excavation, backfill, compaction, and concrete reinstatement. When the scope sheet for the plumbing sub does not specify trench scope, the sub excludes it. The GC finds out during buyout.


This is one of the most consistent gaps in MEP bid packages at mid-market GCs. The fix is a single line in the scope sheet. The miss can cost $40K–$80K on a mid-size commercial project.


### 5. Lighting Controls and BAS Integration


Lighting control specifications have migrated to networked systems over the past decade. The electrical drawings show fixture locations and circuit homerun points. The spec section for lighting controls describes a BAS-integrated system with a separate controls contractor, proprietary software, and commissioning requirements.


When the electrical scope sheet goes out without calling this out explicitly, the sub prices standard switching. The controls scope is unassigned. On a large commercial project, that gap runs $150K–$300K depending on the system complexity.


### 6. Plumbing Rough-In vs. Equipment Connection


This gap appears at the interface between the plumbing sub and the equipment supplier on projects with commercial kitchens, labs, or medical gas systems. The spec assigns rough-in to the plumbing sub and final connection to the equipment supplier. In practice, both parties read the spec differently and each excludes the final tie-in.


The $45K stone-depth mismatch documented in Provision's operator research is a structural parallel. Two disciplines drawing to different reference points, with no one reconciling the interface.


## How MEP Scope Gaps Get Started


Most MEP gaps trace back to one of four root causes. Understanding the cause tells you where to look in the documents.


### Specification Sections Written Before Final Design


Specifications are often written from master spec templates and issued with the bid set before the design is finalized. The engineer-of-record updates the drawings through multiple design development rounds. The spec section does not always follow. The result: the spec references equipment that was substituted in the drawings two months earlier.


### Inter-Discipline Coordination Gaps in the Design Team


On design-bid-build projects, the mechanical, electrical, and plumbing engineers coordinate through the architect. That coordination is imperfect. Interface items such as condensate drain routing, electrical power to mechanical equipment, and plumbing connections for HVAC coils fall into gaps between discipline drawings.


### Addenda That Override Specs Without Updating Drawings


Addenda are the single most common source of document inconsistency on a bid set. An addendum that revises an equipment schedule in the spec does not automatically update the electrical single-line. An addendum that revises a plumbing fixture type may not update the rough-in detail on the architectural drawings.


Catching addenda conflicts requires reading the original spec section, the revised addendum section, and the corresponding drawing detail together. Under time pressure, this is exactly the step that gets cut.


### The Anti-Pattern: "As Per Plans and Specs"


The single most cited scope anti-pattern in Provision's operator research is scope sheets that read "as per plans and specs" for MEP work. This language assigns responsibility without defining it. Every sub reads it differently. Every sub prices it differently. The GC holds the gap.


A pre-construction lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it clearly: "It's descriptive, bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"


That same contact added: "If you miss anything, they'll bill it."


## A Systematic Approach to MEP Cross-Document Review


The following process is drawn from the eight habits framework in the[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) . It is designed for the 72-hour window before bid day when your team is under the most pressure and the most likely to miss something.


### Step 1: Build the MEP Interface Matrix Before You Touch the Scope Sheet


List every MEP system on the project. For each system, identify which discipline drawing set covers it and which specification division governs it. Note every system that appears in more than one drawing discipline. Those are your highest-risk interface points.


This step takes two hours on a mid-size commercial project. It produces a reference document that your entire pre-construction team can use when cross-checking scope assignments.


### Step 2: Read the Spec Sections the Subs Are Least Likely to Read


Subs read Division 21, 22, 23, 26, and 28. They skim Division 01 (general requirements) and often skip it entirely. Division 01 contains testing and commissioning requirements, temporary utilities assignments, and equipment startup protocols that carry real cost.


Your review process should include Division 01 MEP-related sections as a mandatory check. The generator field conditioning cost and BAS commissioning requirements are almost always in Division 01 or in the front-end of the relevant trade section, not in the body of the spec that subs review most carefully.


### Step 3: Cross-Reference Addenda Against Every Affected Document


For each addendum, identify the primary document it modifies. Then ask: does this change affect any other drawing, spec section, or equipment schedule that was not revised in this addendum?


Document your cross-reference in writing. If an addendum revises the mechanical equipment schedule but the electrical power schedule has not been updated, that is a flag. Write it into your pre-bid RFI or call it out as an assumption in your scope sheet.


### Step 4: Run a Trade-Interface Check on Every Scope Sheet


Before a scope sheet goes to any MEP sub, verify three things:


- Every interface item between this trade and adjacent trades is explicitly assigned or explicitly excluded.
- Spec requirements that do not appear on drawings are called out by section number in the scope sheet.
- Testing, commissioning, and startup costs are either included in the scope or assigned to a separate line item in the bid.


This is Habit 1 from the Eight Habits: drawings-first, not boilerplate-first. The scope sheet is built from what the documents actually say, not from what the last similar job included.


### Step 5: Issue a Pre-Bid RFI for Unresolved Conflicts


If your cross-document review finds a genuine conflict between a drawing and a spec (not just an omission, but an actual contradiction), issue a pre-bid RFI. Document the conflict with specific references: drawing number, sheet, detail, and spec section and paragraph.


This protects your bid. If the owner does not respond before bid day, your bid qualifications can reference the open RFI and exclude the disputed scope. That is a defensible position. "As per plans and specs" is not.


### Step 6: Run the Pre-Issue Scope Review Checkpoint


This is Habit 8 from the Eight Habits framework. Before scope sheets go to MEP subs, a senior estimator or pre-construction lead reviews each package against the interface matrix built in Step 1. The review is not a proof check. It is a coverage check: does this scope sheet address every item on the interface matrix?


On a complex MEP project, this review takes 60–90 minutes. It is the step most often cut under bid-day pressure. It is also the step that catches the $150K lighting controls gap before the sub's number is in your bid.

## Protecting Your Bid: What to Do Right Now


You do not need new software to improve your MEP scope review this week. Start with these three changes to your current process.


- **Add an MEP interface matrix to your bid kickoff checklist.** Two hours of structured document review at bid kickoff prevents 20 hours of gap-chasing during buyout.
- **Remove "as per plans and specs" from every MEP scope sheet template.** Replace it with specific document references: drawing number, spec section, and paragraph. This is Habit 2 from the[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) .
- **Schedule the pre-issue scope review checkpoint 48 hours before bid day.** Not the morning of. Not the night before. 48 hours gives you time to catch something and act on it.


MEP scope gaps are not random. They are produced by specific document coordination failures and specific review shortcuts. Fix the process, and you fix the margin.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is an MEP scope gap in construction?


An MEP scope gap is a requirement that appears in the mechanical, electrical, or plumbing bid documents (drawings, specs, or both) but is not assigned to any sub in the scope of work. These gaps surface during buyout or field execution as change orders. They are most common at the interface between disciplines or between drawing sets and specification sections.


### Why do drawings and specs conflict on MEP work?


Drawings and specs are authored by different engineers on different timelines. Specs are often written from master templates before design is final. Drawings evolve through multiple revisions. When addenda revise one document but not the other, conflicts result. MEP work has the highest density of cross-discipline interfaces, so conflicts are more common than in other trades.


### What MEP items are most commonly missed in bid scopes?


Generator field conditioning, motor starters and VFDs, fire-rated louvres, plumbing trench scope, lighting controls and BAS integration, and final equipment connections are the most frequently missed items. Each one shares the same root cause: the requirement lives in a specification section that does not appear on any drawing.


### How do I protect a bid when drawings and specs conflict?


Issue a pre-bid RFI with specific document references (drawing number, sheet, spec section, and paragraph). If the owner does not respond before bid day, include a bid qualification that references the open RFI and excludes the disputed scope. "As per plans and specs" is not a defensible position when the plans and specs say different things.


### How long does a proper MEP cross-document review take?


On a mid-size commercial project with 400–800 drawing sheets and a standard spec book, a structured MEP interface review takes 8–16 hours for a senior estimator. Purpose-built tools like Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) compress this to under 60 minutes by reading the full document set together and generating cited, trade-by-trade scope packages.


### What is the "readily inferable" risk in MEP specifications?


Many contracts include language requiring the GC to provide all work "readily inferable" from the contract documents, even if not explicitly shown. On MEP work, this language can assign spec-based requirements (like generator commissioning or BAS integration) to the GC without a drawing reference. The $300K lead-lined glass gap documented in Provision's operator research was absorbed under exactly this type of clause.
